newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan shakes up cabinet in anti-crime strategy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan shakes up cabinet in anti-crime strategy.

text.p: Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party approved a modest reshuffle of the beleaguered cabinet on Wednesday, hoping an injection of fresh talent would help ease public anger over a perceived breakdown of law and order.

The six appointments, announced by party secretary-general Wu Po-hsiung after a meeting of the party's central standing committee, contained no surprises because a draft list was leaked to local media on Sunday.
As expected, Premier Lien Chan did not heed growing opposition calls for his own resignation. Lien has pledged to resign in July after the constitution is amended.
Wu made no comment as he unveiled the new appointments.

The most significant job of interior minister was given to Yeh Ching-fong. She already had a place in cabinet as a minister without portfolio and becomes the first woman to head the interior ministry, which oversees Taiwan's police.

Incumbent Lin Feng-cheng, who resigned on May 8, had been under fire over a wave of brutal unsolved crimes that has swept the island in recent months -- most recently the kidnap and murder of schoolgirl Pai Hsiao-yen.

Police have also yet to crack the gangland-style execution last November of northern Taoyuan county's magistrate and seven others in his home. Nine people were methodically bound and shot in the head at point-blank range. Only one survived.
Also unsolved is the murder of a feminist opposition politician who was found dead with 35 stab wounds in southern Kaohsiung two weeks after the Taoyuan killings.
The other closely watched portfolio, that of government spokesman, went to David Lee, a career diplomat who recently served as deputy chief of the Government Information Office.
Lee replaces government information office chief Su Chi, who was promoted to minister without portfolio.
A conspicuous hole in the cabinet caused by the unexpected resignation of Nationalist Party "golden boy" Ma Ying-jeou was filled by Chao Shou-po, who has served as secretary-general to the premier.

Ma, who had been justice minister until mid-1996 and more recently a minister without portfolio, said he quit to take responsibility for the cabinet's poor anti-crime work, casting doubt on the party's plans to offer the charismatic Ma as a candidate in future elections.
Ma's departure put an end to speculation that Premier Lien and President Lee Teng-hui would reject his resignation.

Peng Tso-kuei was named to replace Council of Agriculture chairman Tjiu Mau-ying, who resigned to take responsibility for a hog foot and mouth disease epidemic that has ravaged Taiwan's feed lots since March 20.
Hsu Chieh-kwei was named to head the Council of Labour, replacing Hsieh Sheng-shan, who quit to run for magistrate of Taipei county.
